paras: The attempted lynching of Riley Wiggins was an attempt in early August 1882 to lynch a Black hotel cook held in the jail at El Paso, Texas, after he killed two Mexicans who had shot him. Officials kept him safe, and the Dallas Daily Herald reported the case because Wiggins had been a well-known waiter at a Dallas hotel.

Wiggins, known to boarders at the Grand-Windsor hotel in Dallas as "Sam" or "Smiling Sam" and described as "something of a musician," was working as an assistant cook at one of the hotels in El Paso. He was said to have family or relatives in Mansfield, Louisiana.

In the Mexican section of El Paso, Wiggins had "a difficulty with some of his fellows," and pistols were drawn on him. As he ran to escape, "the Mexican boys" fired on him and wounded him in the head. Wiggins fired back and killed two of them.

He was then placed in the El Paso jail, where, in the Herald's words, "they have tried to lynch him, though he is duly cared for by the officials in charge." The report did not say who made the attempt, how many took part, or when it happened.

John McCutcheon, a Black friend of Wiggins in El Paso, wrote to his former fellow-waiters at the Windsor in Dallas asking for assistance. Because Wiggins would be tried "in the Mexican limits, where the killing was done," McCutcheon feared that "full justice will not be done." No report of a trial or its outcome was found in the coverage.

The only account appeared in the Dallas Daily Herald on August 11, 1882, under the headline "A Former Dallas Hotel Waiter in Trouble for Killing at El Paso." Drawing on news from El Paso and McCutcheon's letter, the Herald presented Wiggins as a familiar local figure and gave his side's account, that he was fired on first, without comment. No other white paper's version and no Black-press coverage was found.
